Cabbage family (brassicas).Broccoli: Broccoli's name comes from the Italian for little arms, and Romans bred it from wild cabbage. Eating the florets means eating flower buds before they open.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Cauliflower: Cauliflower is a cabbage bred for its pale, tightly packed flower head. Mark Twain called it a cabbage with a college education.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Kale: Kale was a mainstay in medieval Europe because it survives frost. It stays closest to wild cabbage, with open leaves instead of a tight head.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Brussels sprouts: Brussels sprouts are tiny cabbages that grow along a tall stalk, and they have been grown near Brussels since at least the 1500s. A single plant can bear dozens of them.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Kohlrabi: Kohlrabi is a swollen stem, not a root, and its name means cabbage turnip in German. It tastes like a mild, sweet broccoli stem and is crunchy when raw.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Bok choy: Bok choy is a Chinese cabbage that has been grown in China for over a thousand years. It is a loose-leaf brassica with no tight head.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Collard greens: Collard greens are a headless cabbage relative and a staple of Southern U.S. cooking. Eating them on New Year's Day is said to bring money in the year ahead.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Turnip: Turnips are brassicas, though we eat the root. The leaves, called turnip greens, are edible too, and the plant has been farmed for over 4,000 years.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Arugula: Arugula, also called rocket, is a peppery mustard-family salad leaf. The Romans valued it as an aphrodisiac and used it in love potions.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Watercress: Watercress is a peppery brassica that grows in running streams, and it is among the oldest leaf vegetables eaten by people. Its bite comes from the compounds also found in mustard.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Horseradish: Horseradish is a brassica whose root releases sharp, nose-clearing fumes once cut or grated. Fresh-grated, it loses its kick fast unless it is mixed with vinegar.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Wasabi: Real wasabi is a brassica rooted in Japanese streams and is very hard to farm. Most wasabi paste outside Japan is actually dyed horseradish and mustard.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Romanesco: Romanesco is a chartreuse brassica whose florets spiral in a natural fractal. Each cone is a smaller copy of the whole, which makes it a favorite for math lovers.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Lettuce: Lettuce belongs to the daisy family, not the cabbage family. Ancient Egyptians grew a tall type, and its milky sap once earned it a reputation as a sleep aid.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Spinach: Spinach is related to beets and chard, not cabbage. Popeye's 1930s fame sent U.S. spinach sales up by about a third, and a statue of him stands in Crystal City, Texas.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Chard: Chard is a beet that was bred for leaves instead of roots. Its colorful stems, from rainbow chard, are a sign of its beet family ties, not a cabbage family.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Artichoke: An artichoke is the unopened flower bud of a thistle, in the daisy family. If left alone, it blooms into a big, purple flower.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Celery: Celery belongs to the carrot-and-parsley family, not the cabbage family. Its salty, grassy flavor is often combined with onion and carrot as the base of many soups.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Asparagus: Asparagus is a lily-family plant with edible shoots, nowhere near the cabbage group. A patch can keep producing for 15 years or more once established.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Leek: Leek is an onion relative, so it does not fit the brassicas. Its layered, flat leaves differ clearly from the mustard-family cabbage group.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Endive: Endive is a chicory, part of the daisy family, so it is not a brassica. Belgian endive is grown in darkness, which keeps its leaves pale and mild.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Beet: Beets are in the amaranth family, which includes spinach and chard, not cabbage. The same crop is a major source of the world's sugar, besides sugar cane.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Carrot: Carrots are umbellifers, related to parsley, not brassicas. Early cultivated carrots were purple and yellow, and orange ones were popularized in the Netherlands.
Cabbage family (brassicas).Okra: Okra is a mallow, related to hibiscus and cotton, not a cabbage. Its slimy sap thickens gumbo, and the word gumbo itself may come from a West African word for okra.

Coffee drinks.Espresso: The base for most cafe drinks, made by forcing hot water through finely ground coffee at about nine bars of pressure.
Coffee drinks.Latte: Italian for milk, so ordering a latte alone in Italy may get you a glass of milk. The coffee version is caffè latte.
Coffee drinks.Cappuccino: Named for the brown robes of Capuchin friars. Traditionally it has equal parts espresso, steamed milk and foam.
Coffee drinks.Macchiato: Italian for stained or marked: an espresso with a small dab of milk foam, not a tall caramel drink.
Coffee drinks.Americano: Espresso diluted with hot water. Legend says it was named for American soldiers in Italy who found espresso too strong.
Coffee drinks.Flat white: Both Australia and New Zealand claim this drink, a double ristretto topped with velvety microfoam milk.
Coffee drinks.Cortado: Spanish for cut, as in an espresso cut with a little warm milk to soften its acidity.
Coffee drinks.Mocha: Named for the Yemeni port of Mokha, once a coffee trading hub, it now means coffee mixed with chocolate.
Coffee drinks.Ristretto: Italian for restricted, a short espresso shot that uses less water, giving a sweeter, more concentrated taste.
Coffee drinks.Lungo: Italian for long: an espresso pulled with more water, giving a larger and slightly more bitter cup.
Coffee drinks.Irish coffee: Created by chef Joe Sheridan at Foynes airport in the 1940s for cold, weary transatlantic passengers, with whiskey and cream.
Coffee drinks.Café au lait: French for coffee with milk, traditionally made from drip or press coffee, not espresso, and drunk from a wide bowl at breakfast.
Coffee drinks.Frappuccino: A blended iced coffee drink and a trademark of Starbucks, which bought the name from a Massachusetts coffeehouse in 1994.
Coffee drinks.Chai latte: Spiced tea, made with black tea, milk and spices such as cardamom and ginger, so it has no coffee.
Coffee drinks.Matcha latte: Made from powdered green tea, which brings caffeine and a grassy taste, but no coffee.
Coffee drinks.Hot chocolate: Made from cocoa, Aztecs drank it cold and bitter, and Europeans later added sugar and heat. No coffee.
Coffee drinks.Earl Grey: Black tea scented with bergamot orange oil, so it is tea rather than coffee.
Coffee drinks.Rooibos: A caffeine-free South African red bush tea, not coffee.
Coffee drinks.Horchata: A sweet, creamy drink, made in Mexico from rice and cinnamon, and in Spain from tiger nuts. No coffee.
Coffee drinks.Milkshake: Blended milk and ice cream, which had a start in the 1880s as an alcoholic drink with eggs and whiskey. No coffee.
Coffee drinks.Lassi: A yogurt drink from the Punjab, sweet or salty, sometimes flavored with mango, and not coffee.
Coffee drinks.Yerba mate: An infusion of South American holly leaves, sipped through a metal straw. Caffeinated, but not coffee.
Coffee drinks.Bubble tea: Tea with chewy tapioca pearls, invented in Taiwan in the 1980s. It is tea-based, not coffee.
Coffee drinks.Golden milk: A turmeric milk drink from Ayurvedic tradition, naturally caffeine-free and not coffee.

Animals that can change color.Chameleon: A chameleon changes colour mostly to signal mood and regulate temperature by shifting tiny crystals in its skin, not to camouflage.
Animals that can change color.Octopus: An octopus can change colour and texture in a fraction of a second, even though it's thought to be colour-blind.
Animals that can change color.Cuttlefish: Cuttlefish flash rippling patterns across their skin to hypnotise prey, and can match the checkerboards beneath them.
Animals that can change color.Squid: Squid change colour using chromatophores, and some deep-sea species can produce light with bacteria or their own organs.
Animals that can change color.Arctic fox: The Arctic fox turns from brown in summer to pure white in winter, matching the snow.
Animals that can change color.Snowshoe hare: Snowshoe hares turn white in winter, and when climate change leaves less snow, the white ones stand out.
Animals that can change color.Ptarmigan: The ptarmigan swaps from mottled brown in summer to white in winter, and even its feet grow feathers like snowshoes.
Animals that can change color.Flounder: A flounder starts life like other fish but one eye migrates, and as an adult, it can adjust its colour to match the seabed.
Animals that can change color.Anole: Anoles shift between green and brown, and males flash a dewlap, a bright throat fan, to signal.
Animals that can change color.Stoat: Stoats turn white in winter, when the white fur is called ermine, and was used in royal robes.
Animals that can change color.Seahorse: Seahorses change colour to camouflage and to court mates, and it's the male that carries the eggs.
Animals that can change color.Zebra: Zebras keep their stripes for life, and the pattern doesn't change with season or mood.
Animals that can change color.Panda: Giant pandas keep their black-and-white coat all year with no change.
Animals that can change color.Tiger: Tigers keep their stripes, which don't change colour.
Animals that can change color.Penguin: Penguins have fixed black-and-white plumage, which provides countershading underwater.
Animals that can change color.Crow: Crows are always black, and their colour doesn't shift with season.
Animals that can change color.Giraffe: Giraffes keep their patches throughout their lives, though older males darken with age.
Animals that can change color.Skunk: Skunks have a fixed black-and-white warning coat.
Animals that can change color.Polar bear: Polar bears look white all year, though their fur can appear yellowish in summer; they don't actually change colour.
Animals that can change color.Ladybug: A ladybug's bright warning colours are fixed, although they may fade slightly with age.
Animals that can change color.Dalmatian: Dalmatians are born white and develop spots, a one-time change rather than a flexible one.
Animals that can change color.Parrot: Parrots keep their vivid plumage, which comes from pigments and structure, and doesn't change at will.
Animals that can change color.Elephant: Elephants stay grey, but they often look reddish or brown after dust-bathing in the local soil.
Animals that can change color.Koala: Koalas are grey and don't change colour, though their fur gets a bit lighter on the chest.

Things made from apples.Cider: Fermented apple juice. In the United States, unfermented cloudy apple juice is also called cider, which confuses visitors.
Things made from apples.Calvados: An apple brandy from Normandy, distilled from cider and aged in oak barrels. Some bottles rest for decades.
Things made from apples.Applesauce: Cooked, mashed apples. John Glenn ate applesauce squeezed from a tube in 1962, the first solid food eaten in orbit by an American.
Things made from apples.Apple butter: Apples cooked slowly until they turn dark and spreadable. It has no dairy, and the name refers to its smooth texture.
Things made from apples.Apple cider vinegar: Made by fermenting cider into acid. Cloudy strands in some bottles are called the mother and are harmless.
Things made from apples.Tarte Tatin: Famous upside-down French apple tart, said to have been created by accident by the Tatin sisters when one cooked the pastry wrong way up.
Things made from apples.Apple pie: A symbol of America, though apples are not native to it and the dish came from England. Early colonists brought the trees.
Things made from apples.Applejack: American apple brandy historically made by freeze distillation, leaving the strongest liquid behind as the water froze out.
Things made from apples.Apple crumble: British dessert with a buttery oat or flour topping. It rose in popularity during World War II as a pastry-saving alternative to pie.
Things made from apples.Pommeau: A Normandy blend of apple juice and calvados, aged in oak. It makes a sweet aperitif with about 17 percent alcohol.
Things made from apples.Perry: Made from pears, not apples, though the process is the same as cider. Pear trees can live far longer than apple trees.
Things made from apples.Kirsch: A clear brandy from cherries, not apples. Its name is simply the German word for cherry.
Things made from apples.Slivovitz: A plum brandy popular in the Balkans, not apples. Its name comes from the Slavic word for plum.
Things made from apples.Marmalade: Traditionally made from citrus fruit, especially bitter Seville oranges. Its name goes back to the Portuguese word for quince.
Things made from apples.Mead: Honey wine, not apple. Fermented honey and water is one of humanity's oldest drinks.
Things made from apples.Raisins: Dried grapes. They are sweet enough to ripen without any added sugar.
Things made from apples.Prunes: Dried plums, which are loved as a gentle digestive aid. Plums are related to apples as both belong to the rose family.
Things made from apples.Limoncello: Italian liqueur made by steeping lemon peel in alcohol. The lemons from the Amalfi coast are famous for it.
Things made from apples.Grenadine: A red syrup made from pomegranate juice, not apple, despite its fruity name. It takes its name from the French word for pomegranate.
Things made from apples.Poire Williams: A French pear brandy, sometimes bottled with a whole pear grown inside the bottle. The pears grow in the glass while still on the tree.
Things made from apples.Sake: Brewed from rice, not apples. Many types are best served chilled, though some are warmed.
Things made from apples.Pineapple juice: Pineapple is unrelated to apples, and its name just echoes the old English word for pine cone.
Things made from apples.Pomegranate molasses: A tart syrup of boiled-down pomegranate juice, widely used in Middle Eastern cooking.
Things made from apples.Cranberry sauce: Made from cranberries, a tart North American berry related to blueberries. It is a classic at Thanksgiving.

Island nations.Japan: An archipelago of about 6,800 islands, though four main ones hold nearly all the people. The country sits on the Ring of Fire and has over 100 active volcanoes.
Island nations.Iceland: A volcanic island on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where two tectonic plates are pulling apart. Nearly all its electricity and heat come from hydro and geothermal power.
Island nations.Madagascar: The world's fourth-largest island and a country of its own. Most of its plants and animals, including all lemurs, live nowhere else.
Island nations.Cuba: The largest island in the Caribbean, only about 150 km from Florida. Its old American cars are famous because of decades of import restrictions.
Island nations.Jamaica: A Caribbean island that gave the world reggae and has produced Usain Bolt, the fastest man in history over 100 metres.
Island nations.Sri Lanka: A teardrop-shaped island off India, once called Ceylon. It is the home of famous tea and the Ceylon sapphire.
Island nations.Malta: An archipelago in the Mediterranean, whose Knights of St John defended it in the great siege of 1565. It is one of Europe's smallest and most densely populated countries.
Island nations.Cyprus: The Mediterranean island said to be the birthplace of Aphrodite. It is split by a UN buffer zone, but the Republic of Cyprus is the EU member.
Island nations.New Zealand: Two main islands in the South Pacific; it was the last big land mass settled by humans, around 1300. There are far more sheep than people.
Island nations.Philippines: An archipelago of over 7,000 islands, named for Spain's King Philip II. It is one of the world's most disaster-prone countries, with typhoons and volcanoes.
Island nations.Indonesia: The world's largest island country, with over 17,000 islands. Its people speak hundreds of languages, though they share a single national tongue.
Island nations.Fiji: A South Pacific country of over 300 islands, famed for its resorts. Its fire-walking tradition and its rugby sevens are internationally known.
Island nations.Singapore: An island city-state at the tip of Malaysia, so tiny that it has reclaimed land from the sea to grow by about a quarter since independence.
Island nations.Greenland: A trap: it is an island, the world's largest, but a territory of Denmark, not a nation of its own, though it has broad self-rule.
Island nations.Hawaii: A state of the US, not a country. It is the only American state made up entirely of islands, though it was a kingdom until 1893.
Island nations.Sicily: The largest island in the Mediterranean, but part of Italy. It has been ruled by Greeks, Arabs, and Normans.
Island nations.Tasmania: A large island and state of Australia, not a country. It's home to the Tasmanian devil, and its tigers' last known individual died in 1936.
Island nations.Borneo: The world's third-largest island, but shared between Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei, so no single nation.
Island nations.Corsica: A trap: a Mediterranean island that is part of France, and the birthplace of Napoleon. It is a region of France, not a nation.
Island nations.Bali: A trap: this famous resort island is a province of Indonesia, known for its Hindu temples and rice terraces. It is not its own nation.
Island nations.Sardinia: A trap: the Mediterranean's second-largest island is a region of Italy, with its own language and ancient stone towers.
Island nations.Crete: Greece's largest island and the home of the Minoan civilization, but not a country, so it doesn't fit.
Island nations.Vietnam: A country on the Indochinese mainland, not an island nation, though it has a very long coast.
Island nations.Italy: A peninsula on the mainland of Europe, though it includes islands such as Sicily and Sardinia. Not an island nation.

Things associated with Australia.Kangaroo: A newborn is only about the size of a jellybean when it crawls into its mother's pouch, where it stays for months.
Things associated with Australia.Koala: These marsupials sleep up to 20 hours a day because their eucalyptus diet gives little energy; they are not bears.
Things associated with Australia.Boomerang: Only some Aboriginal Australian designs return when thrown; the heavier hunting types fly straight and were used to bring down game.
Things associated with Australia.Didgeridoo: An Aboriginal wind instrument from northern Australia, traditionally made from a termite-hollowed eucalyptus branch and played with circular breathing.
Things associated with Australia.Vegemite: The salty yeast spread was invented in 1922; it is loved by Australians, and most people spread it very thinly on buttered toast.
Things associated with Australia.Wombat: Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings, which they stack to mark territory because the cubes do not roll away.
Things associated with Australia.Platypus: This egg-laying mammal has a duck-like bill that senses electric fields, and males carry venomous spurs on their hind legs.
Things associated with Australia.Lamington: A sponge cake dipped in chocolate icing and rolled in coconut, probably named after a Queensland governor, Lord Lamington.
Things associated with Australia.Tim Tam: The chocolate biscuit is so loved that Australians invented the 'Tim Tam Slam': bite both ends, then sip hot drink through it like a straw.
Things associated with Australia.Akubra: The felt hat of the Australian outback, made in Tasmania since 1874, whose wide brim keeps the harsh sun off.
Things associated with Australia.Kookaburra: This kingfisher's loud call sounds just like human laughter, and it is often heard at dawn and dusk.
Things associated with Australia.Emu: Australia's tallest bird can run about 50 km/h, and it famously 'won' the 1932 Emu War against soldiers armed with machine guns.
Things associated with Australia.Kiwi bird: This flightless bird is New Zealand's national symbol; it lays one of the largest eggs for its body size of any bird.
Things associated with Australia.Haka: A Maori ceremonial dance with chanting and stamping, performed by the All Blacks before rugby matches; it belongs to New Zealand.
Things associated with Australia.Hobbiton: The Hobbit village set was built near Matamata in New Zealand for Peter Jackson's films, and tourists still visit it.
Things associated with Australia.Moose: The largest member of the deer family lives in northern North America and Eurasia, and it is absent from Australia.
Things associated with Australia.Panda: Giant pandas live only in the mountains of central China, and they eat bamboo for up to 14 hours a day.
Things associated with Australia.Llama: A South American pack animal from the Andes; llamas are used to carry loads and can hum when they are curious.
Things associated with Australia.Lemur: Lemurs live naturally only on Madagascar and nearby islands, and many species are endangered.
Things associated with Australia.Sloth: These slow tree-dwellers of Central and South America can take a week to digest a single leaf meal.
Things associated with Australia.Maple syrup: It takes about 40 liters of sap to make one liter of syrup, and Canada produces most of the world's supply.
Things associated with Australia.Bison: The American bison nearly went extinct in the 1800s, when herds shrank from tens of millions to a few hundred animals.
Things associated with Australia.Hippo: Hippos kill more people in Africa each year than lions do, though they cannot swim and instead walk along river bottoms.
Things associated with Australia.All Blacks: New Zealand's rugby union team, which has won the World Cup three times; they are Kiwi, not Australian, despite the rivalry.

Earthquake vocabulary.Epicenter: The point on the surface directly above where the rupture began. Not to be confused with the hypocenter, which is the actual spot underground.
Earthquake vocabulary.Fault line: A crack in the crust along which rocks slip. California's San Andreas Fault runs for about 1,200 kilometers.
Earthquake vocabulary.Aftershock: A smaller quake following the main one, as the crust adjusts. They can keep going for weeks, months or even years.
Earthquake vocabulary.Richter scale: Charles Richter developed the scale in 1935, with each step representing about 32 times more energy. Scientists now mostly use moment magnitude.
Earthquake vocabulary.Seismic wave: Energy traveling through Earth from a quake. By timing these waves, scientists have even mapped our planet's liquid outer core.
Earthquake vocabulary.Tremor: A shaking of the ground, often small. Some tremors happen deep underground without any strong shock, and are called slow slip events.
Earthquake vocabulary.Foreshock: A smaller quake that comes before a bigger one. You can only tell it was a foreshock afterwards, which makes prediction hard.
Earthquake vocabulary.Hypocenter: The underground point where an earthquake begins. Also called the focus, and its depth affects how damaging the shaking is.
Earthquake vocabulary.Liquefaction: Shaking can make wet, loose soil act like liquid. Buildings can sink or tilt, as happened in Niigata, Japan, in 1964.
Earthquake vocabulary.Seismograph: An instrument that records ground motion. The first was built in China in AD 132 by Zhang Heng, using balls and dragon heads.
Earthquake vocabulary.P-wave: The fastest seismic wave, and the first to arrive. It compresses the ground like a spring, and it can travel through liquids.
Earthquake vocabulary.Eye wall: A ring of towering storm clouds around a hurricane's eye, where the strongest winds blow. It belongs to storms, not quakes.
Earthquake vocabulary.Storm surge: A rise of sea level pushed ashore by a hurricane. It's often the deadliest part of a storm, and it's not quake vocabulary.
Earthquake vocabulary.Funnel cloud: The rotating cloud of a forming tornado. It's a weather term.
Earthquake vocabulary.Wind shear: A change in wind speed or direction with altitude. Pilots dread it during takeoff and landing.
Earthquake vocabulary.Jet stream: Fast rivers of air high in the atmosphere that steer weather systems. They can top 300 km/h.
Earthquake vocabulary.Cold front: The leading edge of a cold air mass, often bringing storms. It's a weather term.
Earthquake vocabulary.Anemometer: A device that measures wind speed, usually using spinning cups. It's a weather tool, not a quake one.
Earthquake vocabulary.Barometer: A tool that measures air pressure. Falling pressure often signals approaching storms.
Earthquake vocabulary.Dew point: The temperature at which air becomes saturated and water condenses. When it's close to the air temperature, it feels muggy.
Earthquake vocabulary.Heat index: The 'feels like' temperature when humidity is combined with heat. It's a weather term.
Earthquake vocabulary.Wind chill: How cold the wind makes the air feel on bare skin. It doesn't change the actual temperature.
Earthquake vocabulary.Isobar: A line on a weather map connecting points of equal pressure. Close-packed isobars mean strong winds.
Earthquake vocabulary.Sea breeze: A cool wind from the sea blowing onto land by day, because land heats faster than water. It's a weather term.

Animals with an exoskeleton.Crab: Crabs wear their skeleton outside and must molt it to grow, hiding in a soft, vulnerable state until the new shell hardens.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Lobster: A lobster molts many times in its first years, and it eats its old shell afterward to recover the calcium.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Beetle: Beetles are the largest group of animals, with roughly 400,000 known species, and their hard wing cases are modified front wings.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Ant: An ant's exoskeleton is light yet strong, helping it carry many times its own weight.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Spider: Spiders have an exoskeleton, and they molt to grow, sometimes looking like a ghostly copy left behind on the web.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Scorpion: Scorpions glow blue-green under ultraviolet light because of compounds in their exoskeleton.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Shrimp: Shrimp are crustaceans, and the shell is shed repeatedly. The shell of a cooked one turns pink as pigment is released.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Grasshopper: Grasshoppers shed their skin about five or six times before becoming adults, with wings forming only at the end.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Cockroach: Cockroaches can live for a week or so without a head, and their tough exoskeleton lets them withstand a lot of pressure.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Tick: Ticks are arachnids, not insects, with a tough exoskeleton that can stretch as they swell when feeding.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Centipede: Centipedes have a segmented exoskeleton, and despite the name, they have anywhere from about 30 to over 300 legs, always an odd number of pairs.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Turtle: A turtle's shell is part of its own skeleton, fused to ribs and spine, so it is an endoskeleton in effect.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Armadillo: An armadillo's armor is bony plates in the skin, covered in keratin. Its skeleton is inside, like ours.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Tortoise: A tortoise shell is made of bone fused to its spine and ribs. It is not an outside skeleton like a crab's.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Octopus: An octopus has no skeleton at all, which lets it squeeze through any gap larger than its beak.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Jellyfish: A jellyfish has no skeleton, being about 95 percent water, and doesn't even have a brain.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Earthworm: An earthworm has no skeleton at all. It moves using fluid pressure inside its body segments.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Starfish: A starfish has hard plates under the skin, which is an internal skeleton, not an outer shell.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Pangolin: A pangolin's scales are made of keratin, like your fingernails, and grow from skin. It has bones inside.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Hedgehog: A hedgehog's spines are modified hairs. It has an internal skeleton like other mammals.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Porcupine: A porcupine's quills are hollow, modified hairs, and not an exoskeleton. It has a normal internal skeleton.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Crocodile: A crocodile's armored skin has bony plates called osteoderms, but its skeleton is on the inside.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Sea urchin: A sea urchin's spiky shell is called a test, and it lies just under the skin, making it an internal skeleton.
Animals with an exoskeleton.Slug: A slug has no shell and no skeleton at all, relying on a muscular body and slime, so it is neither armored nor hard-shelled.

Star Wars planets and moons.Tatooine: Tatooine's name comes from Tataouine in Tunisia, where George Lucas filmed the desert scenes in 1976.
Star Wars planets and moons.Hoth: The ice planet scenes in The Empire Strikes Back were filmed in Norway, near the Hardangerjokulen glacier, in a bitter cold spell.
Star Wars planets and moons.Endor: The forest moon was filmed in California's redwoods, and the Ewok village was built among the giant trees.
Star Wars planets and moons.Naboo: Naboo's lakeside palace scenes in Attack of the Clones were filmed at Villa del Balbianello on Italy's Lake Como.
Star Wars planets and moons.Coruscant: Coruscant is a planet covered by one huge city, and its name comes from 'coruscate', meaning to sparkle.
Star Wars planets and moons.Dagobah: Yoda's swampy home world was a set built on a soundstage in England, and the fog hid its limits.
Star Wars planets and moons.Alderaan: Leia's peaceful world was destroyed by the Death Star in A New Hope, as a demonstration of power.
Star Wars planets and moons.Mustafar: Mustafar is the volcanic planet where Anakin and Obi-Wan duel in Revenge of the Sith, and Darth Vader later made his castle there.
Star Wars planets and moons.Kashyyyk: Kashyyyk, the Wookiee home world, first appeared in the infamous 1978 Star Wars Holiday Special.
Star Wars planets and moons.Jakku: The desert scenes of Jakku in The Force Awakens were filmed in the real dunes near Abu Dhabi.
Star Wars planets and moons.Bespin: Bespin is a gas giant whose Cloud City floats in its atmosphere, and Lando Calrissian runs its mining operation.
Star Wars planets and moons.Kamino: Kamino is the stormy ocean world where the clone army is grown, in Attack of the Clones.
Star Wars planets and moons.Mandalore: Mandalore is the world of the warrior culture whose armor Boba Fett and the Mandalorian wear.
Star Wars planets and moons.Vulcan: Vulcan is Spock's Star Trek home world. In the 1800s, astronomers also hunted a hypothetical planet of that name inside Mercury's orbit.
Star Wars planets and moons.Romulus: Romulus is the Romulan home world of Star Trek, destroyed in the 2009 reboot film.
Star Wars planets and moons.Arrakis: Arrakis, the desert planet of Frank Herbert's Dune, is the only source of the valuable spice melange.
Star Wars planets and moons.Pandora: Pandora is the moon where Avatar takes place, and its name echoes the Greek myth of the first woman and her jar.
Star Wars planets and moons.Gallifrey: Gallifrey is the home world of the Time Lords in Doctor Who, and the Doctor left it long ago.
Star Wars planets and moons.Krypton: Krypton is Superman's lost home world. The chemical element krypton shares the name, meaning 'hidden' in Greek.
Star Wars planets and moons.Asgard: Asgard is the fortress realm of the Norse gods, which Marvel turned into Thor's home world.
Star Wars planets and moons.Cybertron: Cybertron is the robot home world of the Transformers, a toy line built on Japanese Takara designs.
Star Wars planets and moons.Skaro: Skaro is the Daleks' home planet, devastated by a long war between the Kaleds and Thals.
Star Wars planets and moons.Xandar: Xandar is the Nova Corps' capital in Guardians of the Galaxy (2014).
Star Wars planets and moons.Mongo: Mongo is the planet of Flash Gordon, the 1930s comic strip that George Lucas wanted to adapt, which led to Star Wars.

Characters in Ice Age.Manny: The grumpy woolly mammoth who anchors the herd; Ray Romano's deadpan voice suits his gentle, grumpy last-of-his-kind sadness.
Characters in Ice Age.Sid: A sloth, voiced by John Leguizamo, whose lisp became the series' signature comedy. He's the one who first adopts the human baby.
Characters in Ice Age.Diego: A saber-toothed cat voiced by Denis Leary. He begins as a trap-setter for the herd but switches sides, and the real animal is called Smilodon.
Characters in Ice Age.Scrat: The saber-toothed squirrel chasing an acorn. He barely speaks, and the sounds are provided by the film's director, Chris Wedge.
Characters in Ice Age.Ellie: A mammoth who believes she is a possum because possums raised her. Queen Latifah voices her.
Characters in Ice Age.Peaches: Manny and Ellie's daughter, born in the third film. In the fourth film she is a teenager, voiced by Keke Palmer.
Characters in Ice Age.Buck: A one-eyed weasel in the dinosaurs' underground world, voiced by Simon Pegg. His rivalry with the dinosaur Rudy is a highlight of the third film.
Characters in Ice Age.Crash: One of Ellie's possum brothers, voiced by Seann William Scott. He and Eddie behave like reckless teenagers.
Characters in Ice Age.Eddie: The other possum brother, voiced by Josh Peck. Eddie and Crash do everything together and get into trouble together.
Characters in Ice Age.Granny: Sid's cranky grandmother, who appears in the fourth film and was left behind. She turns out to be tougher than he is.
Characters in Ice Age.Soto: The pack leader of the sabertooths in the first film, who sends Diego to capture the human baby. Diego's later loyalty is a betrayal of Soto.
Characters in Ice Age.Shira: A saber-toothed tigress and first mate of Captain Gutt in the fourth film. She is voiced by Jennifer Lopez and switches sides.
Characters in Ice Age.Scratte: A squirrel love interest for Scrat in the fifth film, who has her own love of acorns. She is the first time Scrat meets his match.
Characters in Ice Age.Alex: A lion in Madagascar, not Ice Age. Ben Stiller voiced him, and he is a different big cat than Diego.
Characters in Ice Age.Marty: The zebra in Madagascar, not Ice Age. Chris Rock voiced him, and he is not related to the Ice Age herd.
Characters in Ice Age.Gloria: The hippo in Madagascar, not Ice Age. She is voiced by Jada Pinkett Smith, while Ice Age has Ellie voiced by Queen Latifah.
Characters in Ice Age.Melman: The hypochondriac giraffe in Madagascar, not Ice Age. David Schwimmer voiced him.
Characters in Ice Age.King Julien: The lemur king of Madagascar, not Ice Age. Sacha Baron Cohen voiced him, and his I like to move it song became a hit.
Characters in Ice Age.Skipper: The lead penguin in Madagascar, not Ice Age. The penguins got their own TV series and a spin-off film.
Characters in Ice Age.Mort: A mouse lemur in Madagascar, not Ice Age. His obsession with King Julien's feet is a running gag.
Characters in Ice Age.Blu: The blue macaw in Rio, not Ice Age. Jesse Eisenberg voiced him; he is a domestic bird who can't fly.
Characters in Ice Age.Jewel: The wild macaw in Rio, not Ice Age. Anne Hathaway voiced the adventurous female.
Characters in Ice Age.Rafael: A toucan in Rio, not Ice Age. George Lopez voiced him, and he is one of Blu's friends.
Characters in Ice Age.Hammy: A hyperactive squirrel in Over the Hedge, not Ice Age. Steve Carell voiced him, and his sped-up energy is the joke.

Real people Tom Hanks has played.Chesley Sullenberger: The pilot who landed US Airways Flight 1549 on the Hudson River in 2009 after bird strikes. All 155 aboard survived, in the film Sully.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Richard Phillips: The cargo ship captain taken hostage by Somali pirates in 2009, in Captain Phillips. Phillips' crew is celebrated for its calm.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Walt Disney: Hanks played the entertainer in Saving Mr. Banks, wooing P.L. Travers for the Mary Poppins rights. Disney pursued her for about twenty years.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Fred Rogers: The gentle TV host from Mister Rogers' Neighborhood, in A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood. He wore a cardigan knit by his mother.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Jim Lovell: The astronaut commanding Apollo 13 in the 1995 film, famously reported Houston, we've had a problem after an oxygen tank exploded.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Colonel Tom Parker: Elvis Presley's manager in the 2022 film Elvis. Parker, who was not actually a colonel, was a Dutch immigrant who hid his origins.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Ben Bradlee: The Washington Post editor who published the Pentagon Papers in 2017's The Post. Bradlee ran the paper through Watergate.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Charlie Wilson: A Texas congressman who secretly funded Afghan rebels in the 1980s, in Charlie Wilson's War. He was known for his parties.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.James Donovan: The Brooklyn insurance lawyer who negotiated a Cold War spy swap in Bridge of Spies. He later negotiated the release of Bay of Pigs prisoners.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Forrest Gump: A fictional character in the 1994 film Forrest Gump; it adapts a novel and won Hanks his second Oscar in a row.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Woody: The cowboy doll in Toy Story is a fictional character, not a real person. Tom Hanks has voiced him in four films.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Robert Langdon: The symbologist in The Da Vinci Code is a fictional creation by Dan Brown, not a real person.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Chuck Noland: The FedEx employee stranded on an island in Cast Away is fictional. Hanks lost weight over a year of filming for the role.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Paul Edgecomb: A death-row guard in The Green Mile is a fictional character, based on Stephen King's novel.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Josh Baskin: A boy in a grown man's body in Big is fictional. The film's piano scene at FAO Schwarz is famous.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Captain Miller: The captain in Saving Private Ryan is fictional, though inspired by real WWII soldiers. He leads the search for Ryan.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Viktor Navorski: A stateless man stuck in an airport in The Terminal is fictional, though loosely inspired by Mehran Karimi Nasseri's long stay at Paris's airport.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Andrew Beckett: A lawyer with AIDS in Philadelphia is fictional. Hanks won his first Oscar for the role.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Carl Hanratty: An FBI agent in Catch Me If You Can is a fictional character, the real person being the conman Frank Abagnale.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Jimmy Dugan: A fictional baseball manager in A League of Their Own, whose line There's no crying in baseball is famous.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Frank Abagnale: The conman of Catch Me If You Can was a real person, but Leonardo DiCaprio played him, not Hanks. Hanks played the fictional agent chasing him.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Elvis Presley: The real singer, but in the 2022 film he was played by Austin Butler. Hanks played the manager.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Neil Armstrong: The real astronaut was played by Ryan Gosling in First Man, not Hanks. Hanks played Jim Lovell and narrated the Moon-landing miniseries.
Real people Tom Hanks has played.Mr. Banks: A fictional father in Mary Poppins. In Saving Mr. Banks, Hanks played Walt Disney instead.

Works by Beethoven.Moonlight Sonata: The nickname came after his death from critic Ludwig Rellstab, who compared it to moonlight over Lake Lucerne.
Works by Beethoven.Für Elise: It was not published in his lifetime, and nobody is sure who Elise was.
Works by Beethoven.Ode to Joy: The choral finale of the Ninth Symphony, written when he was almost entirely deaf; its tune later became Europe's anthem.
Works by Beethoven.Eroica: Symphony No. 3 was reportedly dedicated to Napoleon until Beethoven scratched the name out when Napoleon crowned himself emperor.
Works by Beethoven.Emperor Concerto: Piano Concerto No. 5; the 'Emperor' name wasn't his. He wrote it as Napoleon's army shelled Vienna in 1809.
Works by Beethoven.Fidelio: His only opera, which he revised several times before it finally succeeded.
Works by Beethoven.Missa Solemnis: A huge Mass in D, written for an archduke's installation as archbishop but finished years too late for it.
Works by Beethoven.Appassionata: Piano Sonata No. 23, nicknamed after his death. Lenin said it was beautiful music but he couldn't listen too often.
Works by Beethoven.Kreutzer Sonata: Violin Sonata No. 9 was named for a violinist who never played it; it later inspired a Tolstoy novella.
Works by Beethoven.The Four Seasons: Vivaldi wrote it: four violin concertos, one for each season.
Works by Beethoven.Swan Lake: Tchaikovsky composed this ballet, premiered in 1877 and not an instant hit.
Works by Beethoven.Clair de Lune: Debussy wrote it, as part of his Suite bergamasque.
Works by Beethoven.The Magic Flute: Mozart's 1791 opera, premiered just weeks before his death.
Works by Beethoven.Boléro: Ravel's 1928 piece repeats the same melody and rhythm while adding instruments, until the explosive end.
Works by Beethoven.The Nutcracker: Tchaikovsky again, a ballet from 1892 based on a story by E.T.A. Hoffmann.
Works by Beethoven.Messiah: Handel wrote it in about three weeks in 1741, and audiences traditionally stand for the Hallelujah chorus.
Works by Beethoven.Canon in D: Pachelbel wrote it in the 1600s; its chord progression turns up everywhere in pop music.
Works by Beethoven.Rhapsody in Blue: Gershwin's 1924 work opens with a famous clarinet glissando.
Works by Beethoven.The Planets: Gustav Holst wrote this suite of seven orbs, one per planet except Earth.
Works by Beethoven.Gymnopédies: Erik Satie's quiet piano pieces from the 1880s, often cited as early ambient music.
Works by Beethoven.Air on the G String: A 19th-century arrangement of a Bach piece, tweaked so the violin plays it all on one string.
Works by Beethoven.The Blue Danube: Johann Strauss II wrote it in 1866 as a choral piece, and it became Vienna's unofficial anthem.
Works by Beethoven.Peer Gynt: Grieg composed the music for Ibsen's play, including In the Hall of the Mountain King.
Works by Beethoven.Carmen: Bizet's opera was poorly received at its 1875 premiere, and he died months later without seeing its success.

Music streaming services.Spotify: Founded in Stockholm in 2006, it launched in 2008 and grew into the world's biggest music streaming service.
Music streaming services.Apple Music: Launched in 2015, it grew out of Apple's 2014 purchase of Beats Electronics for about 3 billion dollars.
Music streaming services.Tidal: Jay-Z bought it in 2015 and relaunched it as an artist-owned service, pitching lossless, higher quality sound as its main draw.
Music streaming services.Deezer: Founded in Paris in 2007, it was among the first big streamers, and its Flow feature builds an endless personalised mix.
Music streaming services.Pandora: It began as the Music Genome Project, where analysts rated songs on hundreds of traits to match listeners with similar tracks.
Music streaming services.SoundCloud: Launched in Berlin in 2008, it lets anyone upload audio, and many rappers and producers broke out from here before getting signed.
Music streaming services.YouTube Music: It launched in 2018 and can play official tracks, live recordings and fan uploads, so it includes cover versions streamers skip.
Music streaming services.Amazon Music: It is bundled with Prime, and its Unlimited tier offers a huge catalogue in high-definition audio.
Music streaming services.Qobuz: This French service, founded in 2007, built its name on lossless, studio-quality files and pays artists a larger share than most rivals.
Music streaming services.Netflix: It began in 1997 as a DVD-by-mail rental business, and it streams video, not music.
Music streaming services.Hulu: Launched in 2007 as a joint venture of TV networks, it is a video service; the name reportedly means "gourd" or "interlude" in Mandarin.
Music streaming services.Disney+: It launched in November 2019 and signed up over 10 million people in its first day, but it streams films and shows only.
Music streaming services.Instagram: Started in 2010 as a check-in app called Burbn, it was sold to Facebook for about 1 billion dollars in 2012.
Music streaming services.Pinterest: Its name blends "pin" and "interest", and people use it to save visual ideas rather than to stream music.
Music streaming services.Zoom: Video calls from this firm exploded in 2020, but it is a meeting tool, not a place to stream albums.
Music streaming services.Uber: It started in 2009 as UberCab in San Francisco; its app lets you pick Spotify tracks in rides, but it is not a streaming service.
Music streaming services.Airbnb: Founded in 2008, it began when the founders rented air mattresses in their apartment, hence the name Air Bed and Breakfast.
Music streaming services.Duolingo: Its green owl mascot, Duo, has become a meme, but the app teaches languages rather than playing songs.
Music streaming services.Shazam: It identifies a song from a few seconds of audio, but it finds music rather than streaming it. Apple bought it in 2018.
Music streaming services.Audible: Amazon owns it, and it sells audiobooks rather than music, though it feels similar to a streaming app.
Music streaming services.Twitch: Born as Justin.tv's gaming spin-off, it streams live video, mostly games, though musicians also broadcast sets there.
Music streaming services.Snapchat: Its disappearing photos launched in 2011, and it is a messaging app that does not offer a music catalogue.
Music streaming services.LinkedIn: The professional network launched in 2003 and was bought by Microsoft in 2016 for about 26 billion dollars.
Music streaming services.WhatsApp: It lets over two billion people send messages, and Facebook bought it in 2014 for around 19 billion dollars.

Equipment at a fitness gym.Treadmill: Treadmills let you run in place, and the first were invented for prisoners in the 19th century, to be used as a punishment.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Dumbbell: Dumbbells got their name from the bell-like weights used to ring bells silently, hence dumb bells.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Barbell: A barbell is a long bar with weight plates, and an Olympic men's bar weighs 20 kg.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Kettlebell: Kettlebells originated in Russia as counterweights, called girya, and later they became a fitness staple.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Bench press: Bench press benches are a staple of strength training, and the record for a raw press is well over 300 kg.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Rowing machine: Rowing machines mimic the full-body motion of rowing, and they work about 85 percent of your muscles, according to some sources.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Squat rack: The squat rack is a frame with safety bars, so you can lift heavy without a spotter.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Exercise bike: Exercise bikes let you pedal indoors, and spinning classes made them popular in the 1990s.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Elliptical: Ellipticals were introduced in the early 1990s as a low-impact alternative that feels like running.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Yoga mat: Yoga mats are used for floor exercises and stretching, and they are often made of rubber or PVC.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Medicine ball: Medicine balls were used by ancient Greeks, including Hippocrates, as weighted balls for rehab.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Pull-up bar: A pull-up bar builds your back and arms, and the pull-up is among the hardest bodyweight moves.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Cable machine: A cable machine uses pulleys so you can pull from any angle, and resistance remains constant.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Wakeboard: A wakeboard is a short, wide board for being towed behind a boat, and its sport was inspired by surfing and water skiing.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Snowboard: A snowboard is for sliding down snowy slopes, and it came from the 1960s 'Snurfer', a toy that inspired the sport.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Jet ski: Jet skis are personal watercraft that zip across water, and the name is a brand that has become a general term.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Zamboni: A Zamboni resurfaces ice, and the company's inventor, Frank Zamboni, built the first in 1949 for his own rink.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Ski lift: Ski lifts haul skiers up mountains, and they have their own type, such as chairlifts, gondolas, and T-bars.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Pinsetter: A pinsetter is the machine at the end of a bowling lane that resets pins; the first automatic one arrived in the 1950s.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Golf cart: A golf cart carries players around the course, and while its tires are gentle on turf, you won't find one in a gym.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Diving bell: A diving bell is an old underwater chamber, first used for salvage, and it has nothing to do with workouts.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Bowling ball: A bowling ball belongs to the lanes, where regulation balls are up to about 16 pounds, but not in a gym.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Pool cue: A pool cue is for billiards, and the tip is chalked to stop it slipping off the ball.
Equipment at a fitness gym.Surfboard: A surfboard needs waves, and the sport originated in Polynesia, so you won't find one in a gym.

Horse races.Kentucky Derby: Run at Churchill Downs since 1875, it lasts about two minutes, which is why it's nicknamed the most exciting two minutes in sports.
Horse races.Grand National: A steeplechase at Aintree over 30 fences, including famous Becher's Brook; many horses fall, and its finish has drawn millions of TV viewers.
Horse races.Melbourne Cup: Australia's race that stops a nation: held on the first Tuesday of November, with a public holiday in Melbourne.
Horse races.Preakness Stakes: The middle jewel of the US Triple Crown, run in Baltimore, where the winner is draped in a blanket of black-eyed Susans, Maryland's state flower.
Horse races.Belmont Stakes: The longest Triple Crown race, at a mile and a half, and the one that has ended many chances at the Triple Crown.
Horse races.Epsom Derby: Legend says it was named by a coin toss between Lord Derby and Sir Charles Bunbury; many races worldwide now borrow its name.
Horse races.Royal Ascot: A week of racing in June where the Royal Family arrives by carriage, and a strict dress code applies in the Royal Enclosure.
Horse races.Cheltenham Gold Cup: The jumping season's blue-riband race, a steeplechase of about three and a quarter miles run each March.
Horse races.Breeders' Cup: A two-day series of championship races staged at a different US track yearly; it attracts top horses from around the world.
Horse races.Dubai World Cup: One of the world's richest races, with a prize fund of about 12 million US dollars, run on a dirt track in the desert.
Horse races.2000 Guineas: Britain's first Classic of the season, run at Newmarket; despite the name, its prize fund is far more than 2,000 guineas now.
Horse races.Tour de France: A cycle race, not horses: more than 3,000 km over three weeks, with riders vying for a yellow jersey.
Horse races.Daytona 500: This Florida car race opens NASCAR's season; its name comes from the number of miles, and it runs 200 laps.
Horse races.Indy 500: A 500-mile car race on the Indianapolis oval; winners traditionally drink milk in Victory Lane.
Horse races.Le Mans: The 24 Hours of Le Mans is a car endurance race in France, where teams share the driving through a full day and night.
Horse races.Iditarod: A sled-dog race of about 1,000 miles across Alaska, commemorating a 1925 serum run to Nome during a diphtheria outbreak.
Horse races.Boston Marathon: The world's oldest annual marathon, first run in 1897, and runners must hit a qualifying time to enter.
Horse races.The Boat Race: Oxford versus Cambridge rowing crews on the Thames, held since 1829; the course is about 4 miles long.
Horse races.America's Cup: Sailing's most famous trophy: yachts, not horses, racing for a prize that has been contested since 1851.
Horse races.Isle of Man TT: A motorcycle race on public roads, running since 1907 and famously dangerous, with riders reaching over 200 mph.
Horse races.Monaco Grand Prix: A Formula 1 race through the narrow streets of Monte Carlo; overtaking is so hard that qualifying often decides the winner.
Horse races.Dakar Rally: An off-road race for cars, trucks and bikes, which began as Paris-Dakar in 1978 and now crosses Saudi Arabia.
Horse races.Giro d'Italia: Italy's three-week cycling race, where the leader wears a pink jersey, the colour of the sponsoring newspaper's pages.
Horse races.Ironman: A triathlon of a 3.8 km swim, 180 km bike ride and full marathon, with the first held in Hawaii in 1978.

Paper crafts.Origami: The Japanese art of folding one sheet of paper without cutting or glue, and a traditional crane is said to grant a wish if you fold a thousand.
Paper crafts.Scrapbooking: Preserving photos and memories on decorated pages, and the hobby took off in the 1980s with acid-free papers to keep photos from yellowing.
Paper crafts.Decoupage: Gluing paper cutouts onto objects and sealing them under varnish, and the name comes from the French for to cut out.
Paper crafts.Papier-mache: Pulped or layered paper hardened with paste, and the French name means chewed paper, because early recipes sounded like it.
Paper crafts.Quilling: Rolling thin paper strips into coils and shapes, and it began with nuns who used gold-edged paper scraps in the Renaissance.
Paper crafts.Card making: Making greeting cards by hand with stamps, folds and layers, and the first Christmas card was sent in London in 1843.
Paper crafts.Kirigami: A cousin of origami that allows cutting, and the name means cut paper in Japanese, so pop-up cards are examples.
Paper crafts.Bookbinding: Stitching pages into a spine, and this craft is older than printing, going back to ancient scrolls and codices.
Paper crafts.Collage: Gluing scraps into a new picture, and the word comes from the French for gluing, popularized by Picasso and Braque around 1912.
Paper crafts.Paper marbling: Floating ink on a thickened liquid to make swirling patterns, and the style is known as ebru in Turkey.
Paper crafts.Paper cutting: Cutting detailed designs from a sheet, and the Chinese version, jianzhi, is used in window decorations at the New Year.
Paper crafts.Knitting: Looping yarn with needles, and it's textile work, not paper craft, though yarn bombing blurs the line.
Paper crafts.Crochet: A single hook pulls loops through loops, and it's a yarn craft, so no paper is needed.
Paper crafts.Pottery: One of humanity's oldest crafts, shaping clay and firing it, and the oldest known pots are about 20,000 years old.
Paper crafts.Woodturning: Shaping wood on a lathe, and the earliest lathes date back to ancient Egypt, with no paper in sight.
Paper crafts.Macrame: Knotting cord into patterns without a loom, and sailors used it to pass time at sea.
Paper crafts.Embroidery: Decorating cloth with thread, and the Bayeux Tapestry is actually an embroidery, not a woven tapestry.
Paper crafts.Quilting: Stitching layers of fabric together, and it's a textile craft; it's quilling that uses paper, so watch the spelling.
Paper crafts.Glassblowing: Shaping molten glass with a pipe and breath, and it was invented around the first century BC, near Syria.
Paper crafts.Candle making: Pouring wax around a wick, and it's a wax craft, not paper.
Paper crafts.Soap making: Saponification, a reaction of fat with lye, makes soap, and has nothing to do with paper.
Paper crafts.Whittling: Carving wood with a knife, and it's a woodcraft, not a paper one.
Paper crafts.Weaving: Interlacing threads on a loom is textile work, though weaving with paper strips also exists, so this is a trap of sorts.
Paper crafts.Beading: Stringing beads onto thread or wire, and it's a craft of beads, not paper, although some beads are rolled from paper.

English words named after myth figures.Panic: From Pan, the goat-footed god whose sudden shouts in the wild were believed to send flocks and travelers into blind terror.
English words named after myth figures.Cereal: Named for Ceres, the Roman goddess of grain, who also gives us the word 'cereal' in the breakfast aisle.
English words named after myth figures.Atlas: Map books got their name from the Titan Atlas; Mercator used his image on a collection of maps published in the 1590s.
English words named after myth figures.Tantalize: King Tantalus was punished in the underworld, standing in water that receded and under fruit just out of reach.
English words named after myth figures.Hypnosis: From Hypnos, the Greek god of sleep, who is the brother of Thanatos, death.
English words named after myth figures.Odyssey: Homer's epic about Odysseus's ten-year journey home now means any long, adventurous trip.
English words named after myth figures.Volcano: From Vulcan, the Roman god of fire and smithing, whose forge was thought to lie beneath Mount Etna.
English words named after myth figures.Nemesis: The Greek goddess of retribution gave her name to the archrival who can't be beaten, or a downfall that was deserved.
English words named after myth figures.Museum: From the Muses, the nine goddesses of the arts and sciences; a 'mouseion' was a place sacred to them.
English words named after myth figures.January: Named for Janus, the Roman two-faced god of doorways and beginnings, who looks both back and ahead.
English words named after myth figures.Herculean: From Hercules, the Roman name of Heracles; it describes a task requiring enormous strength, like his Twelve Labors.
English words named after myth figures.Thursday: Named for Thor, the Norse god of thunder; the Romans knew it as Jupiter's day, 'dies Iovis'.
English words named after myth figures.Mentor: In the Odyssey, Mentor was an old friend of Odysseus, and Athena took his form to guide Telemachus.
English words named after myth figures.Banana: A trap: this likely comes from a West African word, probably Wolof, not from a myth.
English words named after myth figures.Robot: A trap: it comes from the Czech 'robota', meaning forced labor, from Karel Capek's 1920 play.
English words named after myth figures.Algebra: A trap: it's from the Arabic 'al-jabr', meaning reunion of broken parts, from a 9th-century book by al-Khwarizmi.
English words named after myth figures.Shampoo: A trap: it comes from the Hindi 'champo', meaning to press or knead, and arrived in English in the 1700s.
English words named after myth figures.Kindergarten: A trap: German for 'children's garden', coined by Friedrich Froebel in 1840 for his play-based school.
English words named after myth figures.Ketchup: A trap: it likely comes from a Hokkien word, ke-tsiap, for a fermented fish sauce.
English words named after myth figures.Tsunami: A trap: Japanese for 'harbor wave', coined by fishermen who found the wave only after returning to port.
English words named after myth figures.Safari: A trap: it came into English from Swahili, which got it from Arabic 'safar', meaning journey.
English words named after myth figures.Zero: A trap: it came via Italian from Arabic 'sifr', which also gave English the word 'cipher'.
English words named after myth figures.Pajamas: A trap: the word came from Hindi and Urdu 'pae jama', meaning leg garment, via British colonials in India.
English words named after myth figures.Igloo: A trap: from Inuit 'iglu', meaning house, and only some Inuit groups built snow houses as winter shelters.

US Founding Fathers.George Washington: He led the Continental Army, then presided over the Constitutional Convention, and as president he voluntarily stepped down after two terms.
US Founding Fathers.Thomas Jefferson: Principal author of the Declaration of Independence, he died on July 4, 1826, the document's 50th anniversary, hours before John Adams.
US Founding Fathers.Benjamin Franklin: Printer, scientist and diplomat, he was the oldest signer of both the Declaration and the Constitution, and he secured French support during the war.
US Founding Fathers.John Adams: He nominated Washington to lead the army and became the second president. His son John Quincy Adams later became the sixth.
US Founding Fathers.Alexander Hamilton: Born in the Caribbean, he became the first Treasury Secretary and wrote most of the Federalist Papers. He died in a duel with Aaron Burr in 1804.
US Founding Fathers.James Madison: Often called the Father of the Constitution, he drafted the Bill of Rights and was the fourth president, standing only about 5'4".
US Founding Fathers.John Jay: He co-wrote the Federalist Papers and was the first Chief Justice of the United States, serving from 1789 to 1795.
US Founding Fathers.Samuel Adams: An organizer of the Boston Tea Party and cousin of John Adams, he stirred up resistance to British rule. The beer is named for him, though he was a maltster, not a brewer.
US Founding Fathers.John Hancock: President of the Continental Congress, he signed the Declaration in large bold handwriting, so his name still means 'signature' in the US.
US Founding Fathers.Patrick Henry: His 1775 speech ending 'Give me liberty, or give me death!' rallied Virginia, and he later governed the state.
US Founding Fathers.Abraham Lincoln: Trap: he led the nation during the Civil War in the 1860s, about 80 years after the founding generation.
US Founding Fathers.Theodore Roosevelt: Trap: president from 1901 to 1909 and famous for national parks and the Panama Canal, so a century after the founding.
US Founding Fathers.Ulysses S. Grant: Trap: a Union general in the Civil War and then president from 1869 to 1877, many decades after the founding.
US Founding Fathers.Andrew Jackson: Trap: he fought at the Battle of New Orleans in 1815 and became president in 1829, so he belongs to the next generation.
US Founding Fathers.Robert E. Lee: Trap: this Confederate general was born in 1807, after the founding era, though his father fought in the Revolution.
US Founding Fathers.Frederick Douglass: Trap: born into slavery around 1818, he became a leading abolitionist and writer in the 1800s, well after the founding.
US Founding Fathers.King George III: Trap: he was the British king against whom the colonies rebelled, so he was on the other side, not a founder.
US Founding Fathers.Benedict Arnold: Trap: a brilliant American general who turned traitor in 1780 and joined the British, so he is not a founder.
US Founding Fathers.Davy Crockett: Trap: the frontiersman and congressman died at the Alamo in 1836, so he belongs to a later generation.
US Founding Fathers.Daniel Boone: Trap: a frontiersman who blazed the Wilderness Road into Kentucky in the 1770s, famous but not a political founder.
US Founding Fathers.Christopher Columbus: Trap: he reached the Americas in 1492, nearly 300 years before American independence.
US Founding Fathers.Pocahontas: Trap: she lived in the early 1600s in Virginia, about 170 years before the founding.
US Founding Fathers.John F. Kennedy: Trap: president from 1961 until his assassination in 1963, about 180 years after the Founders.
US Founding Fathers.Thomas Edison: Trap: a prolific 19th-century inventor, holder of over a thousand US patents, born in 1847, long after the Founders.

Things you'd find on a desk.Stapler: The red Swingline stapler became a cult prop in the 1999 film Office Space, so its fans were nearly a movement.
Things you'd find on a desk.Mouse pad: Mouse pads gained popularity because ball mice clogged with desk grit, and optical mice later made them mostly optional.
Things you'd find on a desk.Desk lamp: The Anglepoise lamp was designed in the 1930s by George Carwardine, using spring tension to copy the balance of a human arm.
Things you'd find on a desk.Pen holder: A pen holder keeps pens upright, so a desk can look tidy.
Things you'd find on a desk.Monitor: Monitors have moved from the squarer 4:3 shape to widescreen 16:9, and now to ultrawide.
Things you'd find on a desk.Keyboard: The QWERTY layout dates to the 1870s Sholes and Glidden typewriter, and it has outlived every mechanical reason for it.
Things you'd find on a desk.Notepad: The yellow legal pad is credited to Thomas W. Holley, who bundled scrap paper around 1888.
Things you'd find on a desk.Paperweight: Victorian glass paperweights, with flowers sealed inside, are collectible.
Things you'd find on a desk.Calendar: The Gregorian calendar, adopted in 1582, skipped ten days to realign the seasons.
Things you'd find on a desk.Sticky notes: Sticky notes often cling to monitors, a use no one planned.
Things you'd find on a desk.Inbox tray: An inbox tray holds papers waiting, and an empty one is a rare joy.
Things you'd find on a desk.Bathtub: Heavy cast-iron tubs can weigh around 150 kilograms, so no desk would survive one.
Things you'd find on a desk.Lawnmower: A lawnmower belongs in the garage, and the first one was patented in 1830.
Things you'd find on a desk.Refrigerator: A refrigerator belongs in the kitchen, and it won't fit under a desk.
Things you'd find on a desk.Shower head: Many water-saving shower heads use about 7 to 9 liters per minute, but they belong in the bathroom.
Things you'd find on a desk.Toilet: Sir John Harington invented a flush toilet in 1596 for Queen Elizabeth I, though it didn't belong on a desk.
Things you'd find on a desk.Garden hose: A garden hose belongs outdoors, and a desk is no place for one.
Things you'd find on a desk.Wheelbarrow: The Chinese invented the wheelbarrow about 2,000 years ago, and it still belongs on a building site.
Things you'd find on a desk.Ironing board: Ironing boards stay near the laundry, and Sarah Boone patented an improved one in 1892.
Things you'd find on a desk.Car tire: Dunlop's pneumatic tire arrived in 1888 and belongs on wheels, not desks.
Things you'd find on a desk.Sofa: A sofa belongs in the living room, from the Arabic suffa.
Things you'd find on a desk.Bunk bed: A bunk bed is for bedrooms, not offices.
Things you'd find on a desk.Ceiling fan: Philip Diehl invented the electric ceiling fan in 1887, so it looks down on a desk from above.
Things you'd find on a desk.Washing machine: A washing machine belongs in the laundry, and the first electric one was sold in 1908.

Manicure tools.Nail clippers: The first modern nail clippers were patented in the 1880s, and the lever design gives you far more cutting force than the squeeze.
Manicure tools.Nail file: Nail files are used for shaping, and experts suggest filing in one direction to avoid splitting the nail.
Manicure tools.Cuticle pusher: A cuticle pusher gently moves back the skin at the nail base, and soaking your hands first makes it easier.
Manicure tools.Nail polish: Nail polish came from car paint: the first modern polish in the 1920s was inspired by automobile lacquer.
Manicure tools.Nail buffer: A buffer smooths ridges on the nail surface, which makes a natural shine without any polish at all.
Manicure tools.Toe separator: Toe separators hold your toes apart so a pedicure's polish doesn't smudge, and they're made of soft foam.
Manicure tools.Nail scissors: Nail scissors have curved blades that follow the shape of the fingertip, to give a round shape.
Manicure tools.Emery board: An emery board is a card coated with emery, a gritty mineral mixed with corundum, and the name stuck even if modern ones use other grit.
Manicure tools.Cuticle oil: Cuticle oil often contains jojoba, and it keeps the skin around the nail soft and cuts down on hangnails.
Manicure tools.Polish remover: Many nail polish removers contain acetone, a solvent that dissolves polish but can dry out the nails.
Manicure tools.Top coat: A top coat is a clear layer over color that adds shine and helps keep a manicure from chipping.
Manicure tools.Eyelash curler: An eyelash curler is a makeup tool, not for nails, and it was patented in the 1920s by Kurlash.
Manicure tools.Lipstick: Lipstick is a cosmetic for lips, and a modern tube started with the 1915 metal case from the US.
Manicure tools.Mascara: Mascara goes on the eyelashes, and the first modern version came from Maybelline, named after founder's sister Mabel.
Manicure tools.Hairbrush: A hairbrush is for hair care, and it was invented well before the nail polish industry, with natural bristles in the early days.
Manicure tools.Razor: A razor is for shaving, and the disposable safety razor was invented by King Camp Gillette around 1901.
Manicure tools.Toothbrush: A toothbrush cleans teeth, and the first nylon-bristled one went on sale in 1938.
Manicure tools.Comb: Combs are one of the oldest tools, and some date back over 5,000 years, but they do not belong in a manicure.
Manicure tools.Lip balm: Lip balm protects lips, and it's famously sold in tiny tubes, with a number of brands around, but it's not for nails.
Manicure tools.Hair clip: A hair clip holds hair back, so it belongs with hair care, not manicure sets.
Manicure tools.Blush: Blush adds color to the cheeks, and in the past people used crushed fruit or rouge for the same effect.
Manicure tools.Shaving brush: A shaving brush whips up lather, and the best ones were traditionally made from badger hair.
Manicure tools.Eyeliner: Eyeliner is much older than you'd think: ancient Egyptians wore kohl around their eyes, for style and for sun glare.
Manicure tools.Bobby pin: The bobby pin is a flat spring clip for hair, and its name might come from the bobbed haircuts of the 1920s.

Body systems: the ___ system.Nervous: Signals along your fastest nerve fibers travel over 100 meters per second, which is why you yank your hand from a hot stove before you feel the pain.
Body systems: the ___ system.Digestive: Laid end to end, your digestive tract is roughly 9 meters long, and the stomach's acid is strong enough to dissolve metal like zinc.
Body systems: the ___ system.Skeletal: Babies are born with about 300 bones that fuse into 206 in adults, and the skeleton quietly renews itself over roughly ten years.
Body systems: the ___ system.Muscular: Your body has over 600 muscles, yet the quickest-working ones are the tiny muscles that move your eyes.
Body systems: the ___ system.Respiratory: Your lungs hold hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs, and their combined surface could cover a large part of a tennis court.
Body systems: the ___ system.Circulatory: Your heart pumps about 7,000 liters of blood a day through vessels that, laid end to end, would circle Earth more than twice.
Body systems: the ___ system.Immune: Your immune system keeps a memory of past invaders, which is exactly why vaccines work: they give it a safe rehearsal.
Body systems: the ___ system.Endocrine: This hormone network, run by glands like the thyroid and pituitary, steers growth, mood and metabolism by chemical messages in the blood.
Body systems: the ___ system.Lymphatic: It drains fluid from tissues and houses infection-fighting white cells. Unlike blood, lymph has no heart-like pump and relies on muscle movement.
Body systems: the ___ system.Urinary: Your kidneys filter all your blood many times a day, producing only about one to two liters of urine from some 180 liters filtered.
Body systems: the ___ system.Integumentary: Skin, hair and nails form this system, and skin is your largest organ, weighing around 4 kilograms in an adult.
Body systems: the ___ system.Reproductive: It's the only body system not needed to keep an individual alive, existing instead to pass on the species.
Body systems: the ___ system.Solar: Our solar system is a planetary system, not a body system. The Sun holds over 99 percent of all its mass.
Body systems: the ___ system.Metric: A trap, since the metric system measures things rather than bodies. Only the US, Liberia and Myanmar have not officially adopted it.
Body systems: the ___ system.Operating: An operating system runs a computer, not a body. Only the surgeon's operating room would count as body-related, and that's a place.
Body systems: the ___ system.Decimal: The decimal system counts in tens, likely because we have ten fingers, but it's a number system, not an organ system.
Body systems: the ___ system.Binary: Computers rely on the binary system of 0s and 1s. Nothing in the human body is organized this way as a named system.
Body systems: the ___ system.Feudal: The feudal system tied medieval peasants to lords who owed loyalty to kings. It organized society, not anatomy.
Body systems: the ___ system.Sound: A sound system means speakers and amps, not anatomy. Your ears do handle hearing, though, as part of the nervous system.
Body systems: the ___ system.Postal: The postal system delivers mail rather than blood or nerve signals, though Persian and Roman couriers were early versions of it.
Body systems: the ___ system.Honor: The honor system relies on trust instead of enforcement, such as unattended farm stands where you leave money in a box.
Body systems: the ___ system.Buddy: The buddy system pairs divers or hikers for safety. It's a safety practice, not something inside your body.
Body systems: the ___ system.Filing: A filing system organizes paperwork. Your body does its own organizing, with DNA compactly folded inside each cell.
Body systems: the ___ system.Number: A number system, like Roman numerals or base ten, is mathematical. Roman numerals had no symbol for zero.
